title: Surfaces And Riemannian Geometry
notes: Open by shifting the course from moving points to moving coordinate patches. The source span covers printed pages 87 through 103, where the central question is how a parametrized surface inherits measurements. Keep attention on what can be tested: tangent vectors, metric coefficients, area density, and isometry.

title: A Surface Patch Is A Map
notes: Present the parametrization as a machine that takes two coordinates and returns a point in space. The picture should not be treated as the definition by itself. The useful data are the map, the coordinate directions, and the way small rectangles in the domain are pushed into the ambient space.

title: Regular Means Rank Two
notes: Emphasize that a smooth image can still fail as a surface patch if the two partial derivative vectors become dependent. The cross product is the local alarm bell in three dimensions. When it vanishes, the coordinate net has collapsed and metric or area formulas no longer describe a genuine tangent plane.

title: The Tangent Plane Comes From Pushforwards
notes: Use this slide to make the tangent plane feel constructed rather than guessed. The coordinate basis vectors in the parameter domain are pushed forward to X_u and X_v, and their span is the first-order approximation to the patch. Every later measurement is made inside this moving plane.

title: The First Fundamental Form Measures Vectors
notes: Introduce the metric matrix as a compact record of dot products. A coordinate vector a du plus b dv has squared length obtained by multiplying through G. This is the moment where the surface becomes Riemannian: the patch now carries its own ruler for tangent vectors.

title: Metric Ellipses Reveal Distortion
notes: Compare the ordinary unit circle in coordinates with the unit vectors measured by the induced metric. If the ellipse is stretched or tilted, coordinates are not orthonormal. Students should read the ellipse as a diagnostic for lengths and angles, not as decoration on the surface.

title: Area Is The Metric Determinant
notes: Move from lengths to area by drawing the parallelogram spanned by X_u and X_v. Its area is the square root of EG minus F squared, which also equals the norm of the cross product. This formula is the local conversion rate from coordinate area to surface area.

title: Metric Rotation Encodes Orientation
notes: Explain J as a ninety-degree rotation that belongs to the metric, not necessarily to the drawn coordinate grid. The checks J squared equals minus the identity and J preserves G are the algebraic signature of an oriented Riemannian tangent plane. The diagram separates coordinate arrows from measured rotation.

title: Change Coordinates, Preserve Geometry
notes: A reparametrization may shear or stretch the visible grid, but it should not change intrinsic measurements when handled correctly. The Jacobian of the coordinate change transforms the metric matrix. This slide prepares students to distrust raw coordinate spacing while trusting transformed metric data.

title: Isometry Means The Same Metric Data
notes: Define isometry through preservation of the first fundamental form rather than through visual similarity. Two surfaces may sit very differently in space, yet tangent lengths and angles agree after the right correspondence. The central test is whether pullback metric coefficients match, not whether drawings look alike.

title: Plane And Cylinder Calibrate Isometry
notes: Use the plane-to-cylinder example as the clean calibration case. Rolling a flat sheet into a unit cylinder bends the embedding, but the local metric in the unrolled coordinates remains du squared plus dv squared. This helps students separate bending in space from intrinsic stretching.

title: Sphere Coordinates Change The Ruler
notes: The sphere shows why coordinate formulas matter before curvature is introduced. Longitude lines crowd together near the poles, and the metric coefficient for the angular direction carries a sine squared factor. Area density also changes with latitude, so equal coordinate rectangles need not have equal surface area.

title: Notebook Checks Make The Pictures Accountable
notes: Tie the lecture back to the assigned notebook artifacts. The checks are not administrative; they are mathematical witnesses. Positive definiteness keeps tangent lengths real, the area identity verifies the determinant formula, metric rotation tests the orientation operator, and matched examples check whether isometry claims survive computation.

title: Pitfall: Trusting The Drawing First
notes: Warn that a surface plot can look smooth while the determinant of the metric becomes dangerously small. The drawing is a hypothesis generator; the metric determinant is the test. Students should learn to ask where the coordinate grid is nearly singular before believing any area or angle measurement.

title: Applied Lab: Perturb And Recompute
notes: Frame the lab as a controlled debugging exercise. Change one parameter, recompute the partial derivatives, rebuild the metric, and inspect residuals before interpreting the picture. The valuable outcome is not only a passing check; a failing residual identifies which hypothesis of the geometric statement has been broken.

title: Recap: From Patch To Intrinsic Geometry
notes: Close with the dependency chain that the rest of the surface chapters will reuse. A regular patch gives tangent vectors, dot products give the metric, the determinant gives area, orientation gives J, and matching metric data gives isometry. Later curvature and variation build on this local measurement engine.
